text.title: Growth Loops Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every Growth Loops application MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The spec MUST name the four stages (input, action, output, fuel-back) and state explicitly, with a tracked event, how the output of one cycle becomes the input of the next, counted in the same unit at both ends (new users in, new users out; content pieces in, content pieces out). A design whose output does not feed its own input is a funnel and MUST be labelled as one, not as a loop.

rationale.source: Brian Balfour, Reforge, 'Growth Loops are the New Funnels' (2018)

rule.rationale: Most "loops" submitted are funnels with an arrow drawn back to the top. The distinguishing test is the reinvestment event: if nobody can name the event where an output becomes a new input, the compounding the projection promises does not exist and the spec is a funnel with better vocabulary.

rule.statement: The spec MUST declare exactly one primary loop type (viral, user-generated content and search, paid, network effect, or supply-side) and name the input source that type consumes (user action, content, capital, or supply). Secondary loops MAY be listed but MUST NOT be summed into the primary projection.

rationale.source: Brian Balfour, Reforge, 'Growth Loops are the New Funnels' (2018); Andrew Chen, The Cold Start Problem (2021)

rule.rationale: The loop type decides which stage is the constraint and what the loop costs to run: a paid loop is bounded by payback, a content loop by crawl and index rates, a viral loop by invitation behaviour. Blending three loop types into one efficiency number hides which one is actually doing the work and which one is burning cash.

rule.statement: Every stage transition MUST have an instrumented event with a defined numerator and denominator, a measured current value, the measurement date and the sample size behind it. Any stage rate that is an estimate MUST be flagged `assumption` in the metrics table, and a projection that rests on an `assumption` stage MUST say so in its headline.

rationale.source: Widely established practice in growth analytics; templates/growth-loop-design.md.j2 metrics table

rule.rationale: Loop efficiency is a product, so one invented stage rate multiplies through every projection. The pattern that burns quarters is a 30 percent "typical" share rate copied from a blog post standing in for the 4 percent the product actually produces; flagging assumptions is what makes the reviewer ask for the event.

rule.statement: The spec MUST state loop efficiency as the product of the stage conversions (new inputs produced per input, k) and the cycle time (median days from input to fuel-back). If k is below 1 the spec MUST present the loop as an amplifier of external inputs with multiplier 1 / (1 - k) and MUST NOT describe it as self-sustaining; if k is at or above 1 the spec MUST show the cycle-time-bounded growth rate rather than an unbounded curve.

rationale.source: David Skok, 'Lessons Learned: Viral Marketing' (For Entrepreneurs, 2009); Brian Balfour, Reforge, 'Growth Loops are the New Funnels' (2018)

rule.rationale: A loop with k of 0.5 doubles what paid channels bring in, which is valuable and worth funding, but a projection that reads it as "viral" plans headcount for growth that will never arrive. Cycle time is the number teams forget: a k of 1.2 with a 90-day cycle grows slower than a k of 0.7 with a 3-day cycle over a quarter.

rule.statement: The steady-state projection MUST cover at least 90 days and at least three full cycles, be built cohort by cohort with the measured cycle time, and include the decay terms for the loop type (contributor churn, content decay, audience saturation, rising paid CPMs). A projection that extrapolates the first cycle linearly, or that has no decay term, is invalid.

rationale.source: Andrew Chen, The Cold Start Problem (2021), on saturation and ceilings; widely established practice in cohort modelling

rule.rationale: Every loop saturates: invitations reach people already invited, content targets exhausted query space, paid audiences are bid up. A projection without decay produces the hockey stick, funding is committed against it, and the loop flattens in month four exactly where the model said it would not.

rule.statement: The friction map MUST identify the single stage with the lowest conversion as the bottleneck, quantify what doubling that stage does to loop efficiency, and rank optimisation experiments on the bottleneck first. Experiments on a non-bottleneck stage MUST justify why they precede a bottleneck experiment.

rationale.source: Eliyahu Goldratt, The Goal (1984), Theory of Constraints; templates/growth-loop-design.md.j2 bottleneck section

rule.rationale: Because efficiency is a product, doubling the 5 percent stage moves k as much as doubling the 60 percent stage, and doubling 5 percent is far easier. Teams gravitate to the stage they own rather than the stage that constrains, which is how the invite email gets its fourth redesign while the landing page converts at 8 percent.

rule.statement: The spec MUST state blended CAC and CAC payback both with and without loop-sourced users, attributing loop-sourced users only through the tracked fuel-back event, never by relabelling `organic` or `direct` traffic as loop output.

rationale.source: David Skok, 'SaaS Metrics 2.0' (For Entrepreneurs); AGENTS.md trigger condition

rule.rationale: The methodology is invoked because CAC payback is failing, so the spec has to show the loop's effect on that number or it has not answered the question. Counting untracked organic traffic as loop output is the standard way a loop is declared a success without ever proving it moved payback.

rule.statement: The spec MUST define a quality guardrail on loop output with a numeric threshold: loop-sourced users' activation and 30-day retention within a stated margin of the baseline cohort, or for content loops the share of loop-generated pages that are indexed and receive traffic. Loop optimisation that breaches the guardrail MUST be reverted even if k improves.

rationale.source: Andrew Chen, The Cold Start Problem (2021), on spam and quality collapse in viral loops; Google Search Central, 'Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content'

rule.rationale: A viral loop optimised purely on invitations becomes spam and the platform or the inbox provider shuts it off; a content loop optimised on page count fills the index with pages nobody visits and the whole domain is downgraded. The guardrail is the difference between a loop and a mechanism for destroying the brand at scale.

section.title: Conclusion targets used by the decision tree

rule.statement: Run the full procedure; emit an artefact passing the output contract.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when every loop-design signal checks out.

rule.statement: Skip; surface the missing precondition; do not synthesize.
rule.rationale: Terminal target used by 06-decision-tree when no user behaviour produces measurable fuel for new inputs.
